tldr: This study solves the subtle tracking errors that occur when deploying controllers to hardware by cleverly adapting the reference commands fed to the robot, rather than rewriting the policy itself. By modeling the robot and controller together as a single unified system, it achieves high-precision trajectory tracking with just a few dozen finetuning steps on hardware.
hero_caption: The overall architecture of OSRAM. A closed-loop model is meta-trained across randomized physical parameters in simulation, and rapidly finetuned after real-world deployment using a small amount of real data. Using this model, reference commands are adapted via MPPI (sampling-based optimization), requiring no changes whatsoever to the deployed policy.
overview:
Sim-to-real transfer, which transfers control policies trained with reinforcement learning from simulation to hardware, has made great progress. However, a troublesome issue still remains in practice. Even when the robot remains stable and does not fall over, residual tracking errors persist—it subtly drifts from specified velocities or trajectories due to motor delays, friction, and mass discrepancies. Correcting this typically requires re-identifying complex physical parameters on hardware or further training (finetuning) the policy itself, which incurs massive amounts of real-world data and safety verification costs.

The authors therefore took a different angle. They thought: "If the controller is already working stably, why not leave it untouched and instead compensate the reference commands sent to it?" For instance, if the robot tends to lag behind the target velocity, send an intentionally faster command in advance; if it overshoots, ease off early. To perform this compensation accurately, they proposed OSRAM, a framework that treats the robot body and the control policy together as a single "closed-loop system" and directly learns its command-response behavior.

For evaluation, the authors used the bipedal robot "Tron1" and tested it not only on standard velocity tracking but also on a loco-manipulation task with an arm. In both simulation and hardware, OSRAM outperformed conventional domain adaptation methods and residual policy learning in tracking accuracy. In hardware manipulation, it dramatically reduced tracking error (RMSE) from around 37 cm to around 3 cm.
contributions: Formulating the robot and deployed policy as a single closed-loop dynamical system, proposing a framework that directly models task-level command-response behavior rather than high-dimensional physical states.
Meta-training across diverse environment dynamics in simulation (using Reptile) to build a prior model that can immediately adapt after deployment with very little data (a few dozen gradient steps).
Developing an algorithm that uses real-time MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral control) to optimize and adapt reference commands online based on the identified closed-loop model.
Demonstrating significant tracking accuracy improvements on hardware with a bipedal robot across both walking velocity tracking and whole-body loco-manipulation tasks.

sections.heading: Changing the Command, Not the Policy: A New Approach to Sim-to-Real
sections.summary: In sim-to-real transfer, residual tracking errors caused by unmodeled effects like friction and delays remain a major challenge even when the robot runs stably. Instead of retraining the policy, OSRAM treats the entire robot and controller as a black box and optimizes reference commands to cancel out errors.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning has enabled robots to acquire dynamic behaviors, but the sim-to-real gap is still not completely closed. Domain randomization (randomizing simulation mass or friction during training) improves robustness, but widening the distribution too much degrades performance, while keeping it too narrow leaves tracking lags and steady-state errors on hardware.

Another approach is to identify physical parameters from hardware data and retrain the policy. However, accurately estimating physical dynamics on high-dimensional real robots is extremely difficult and requires substantial safety verification costs.

This motivated the idea: "Leave the already functioning controller as is, and adapt the reference commands provided to it instead." For example, if the robot has a habit of running 10% slower than commanded, sending a reference command that is roughly 10% faster from the start should make it run at the desired speed in the end.

To achieve this, OSRAM treats the "robot body + controller" as a single closed-loop dynamical system. Rather than tracking complex full-body joint angles and torques, it only learns the task-space input-output history: "what response came back when a certain command was sent." This enables extremely low-dimensional and data-efficient adaptation.

In (b) loco-manipulation (sine wave tracking), the large tracking lag seen in the baseline is eliminated, closely matching the target trajectory (black dashed line).

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Existing Online Adaptation?
sections.summary: Conventional online adaptation methods (such as RMA or residual policy learning) mainly modify the policy's internal representations or output torques. In contrast, OSRAM leaves the control policy untouched and corrects nonlinear behavior solely through the external reference command interface.
sections.details:
### II-A Online Adaptation for Sim-to-Real Transfer
Methods that adjust behavior using post-deployment data include RMA (Rapid Motor Adaptation), which estimates latent environmental representations from observation history and feeds them to the policy, as well as residual policy learning that adds residual actions on top of a pre-trained policy. However, these require modifying the policy itself or adding extra input modules. In contrast, OSRAM keeps the deployed policy completely frozen and only dynamically transforms the reference commands provided externally, making it extremely easy to integrate into existing systems.

### II-B Input-Output Dynamics Modeling in Robotics
Model-based control that learns state transition models is powerful, but requires massive amounts of data when full-body states are high-dimensional. Therefore, methods that predict future responses from input-output history without fully reconstructing internal states have been proposed (such as NARX models and data-driven reference steering). While prior work on data-driven reference steering often assumes linear representations, OSRAM advances this by leveraging meta-learning in simulation to rapidly adapt nonlinear deep learning models with small amounts of hardware data.

sections.heading: How OSRAM Works: Meta-Learning and Real-Time Sampling Optimization
sections.summary: A closed-loop command-response model is meta-trained across diverse dynamics in simulation. After deployment on hardware, the model is finetuned with minimal real data, and MPPI optimizes the adapted commands in real time at 50 Hz to elicit the desired response.
sections.details:
OSRAM mainly consists of two stages: a meta-learning phase in simulation, and an online adaptation and control phase on hardware.

### Closed-Loop Command-Response Modeling
Treating the combination of the robot and policy $\pi$ as a single system, the model $F_{\theta}$ is defined. This model predicts the next-step real response $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{real}}_{t+1}$ from the past reference command history $\mathbf{r}^{\text{ref}}$ and actual response history $\mathbf{r}^{\text{real}}$. By dealing only with variables directly relevant to the task (such as base velocity or end-effector position) rather than the entire state space, the model's input dimension is drastically compressed.

### Closed-Loop Meta-Learning (Applying Reptile)
To enable rapid adaptation on hardware, OSRAM uses learning inspired by Reptile, a first-order meta-learning algorithm. Inside the simulator, the robot's mass, friction, and actuator characteristics are randomly varied, and excitation signals (perturbations) are added to reference commands to collect diverse data. Training uses a loss function combining a single-step prediction loss and a multi-step autoregressive rollout consistency loss, acquiring initial parameters that adapt to unseen environments with just a few gradient updates.

### Real-Time Reference Command Optimization via MPPI
Once deployed to hardware, the model $F_{\theta}$ is finetuned with a few to several dozen gradient updates using a small amount of trajectory data. Then, the MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) optimization algorithm runs, sampling numerous candidate command sequences in parallel. The evaluation cost incorporates three terms: whether the predicted response tracks the true target ($\ell_{\text{track}}$), whether the adapted command deviates unreasonably from nominal values ($\ell_{\text{dev}}$), and temporal smoothness of commands ($\ell_{\text{smooth}}$). It selects the most appropriate adapted command $\mathbf{r}^{\text{ref,new}}$ and sends it to the controller.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Stable, High-Precision Tracking Even Under Unseen Dynamics
sections.summary: Evaluated on the bipedal robot Tron1 across velocity tracking and loco-manipulation tasks. OSRAM outperformed open-loop models and existing adaptation baselines (RMA-style RNN and residual policies), drastically reducing end-effector tracking RMSE on hardware from 36.94 cm to 3.11 cm.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The experiments used LimX Dynamics' bipedal robot "Tron1" (both standalone and equipped with an arm for loco-manipulation). For control rates, the MPPI planner runs at 50 Hz on an RTX 4090 GPU, and the dynamics model updates in the background at 2 Hz. Evaluation metrics include mean tracking error $E_{\text{mean}}$, root mean square error $E_{\text{RMSE}}$, standard deviation across trials $E_{\text{std}}$, and success rate without falling (SR).

### IV-B Adapting to Unseen Dynamics (Testing Q1)
Under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions with center-of-mass and actuator gains different from training, the proposed meta-model was compared against a standard forward dynamics (FD) model. The 1-step prediction mean absolute error (MAE) dropped from 0.0594 for FD to 0.0116 for the proposed method—a reduction of about 80.5% (roughly one-fifth). This improved prediction accuracy translated directly into control performance, significantly improving RMSE from 0.1472 to 0.0929 at a target velocity of 0.7 m/s.

### IV-C Why Model the "Closed Loop"? (Testing Q2)
OSRAM was compared against standard open-loop models that explicitly take joint actions as inputs (OL-Full using full-body states, and OL-Out using task outputs only). At low speeds, open-loop models managed to work to some extent. However, under a more challenging setting of 0.9 m/s, open-loop model control caused the robot to fall, resulting in a 0% success rate. In contrast, OSRAM, which models the closed loop, maintained a 100% success rate and kept RMSE at 0.1560. When only limited adaptation data is available, modeling focused on "commands and responses" is vastly more robust than predicting low-level actions.

### IV-D Comparison with Existing Online Adaptation Methods (Testing Q3)
OSRAM was compared against latent-estimation (RNN-Adapt, representing RMA) and residual policy (Res-Adapt) methods. While both baselines prevented falls, steady tracking lag remained; at a target velocity of 0.4 m/s, RMSE was 0.1415 for RNN-Adapt and 0.1421 for Res-Adapt. In contrast, OSRAM achieved 0.0733, cutting the error by nearly half.

### IV-E Hardware Verification (Testing Q4)
In hardware experiments, extra weights were intentionally attached and gains altered to create a large sim-to-real gap. In the velocity tracking task, OSRAM notably suppressed lateral wobbling (drift). Prediction error converged after about 30 gradient steps of model finetuning (roughly ten-plus seconds of data).
In the more challenging loco-manipulation task with an arm (tracing a 3D sine wave with the end-effector), the unadapted baseline showed significant lag with an end-effector X-direction RMSE of $36.94\pm 3.02$ cm, whereas applying OSRAM dramatically improved it to $3.11\pm 0.31$ cm.

### IV-F How Are Commands Being Adapted?
Because the prediction model accurately captures real responses, OSRAM generates reference commands that lead the target when the robot has a tendency to lag behind commands. Conversely, if it tends to overshoot, OSRAM pulls back the commands early. By generating these "cleverly biased" commands in real time, the real robot ultimately moves exactly according to the intended target.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Expanding from Low-Dimensional Commands to Whole-Body Coordination
sections.summary: OSRAM is a practical online sim-to-real method that adapts commands through a closed-loop command-response model without changing the policy. Future work includes expanding to high-dimensional whole-body trajectories and leveraging differentiable models for fast gradient-based optimization.
sections.details:
OSRAM demonstrates that residual sim-to-real errors can be eliminated simply by adapting reference commands without modifying existing trained policies. In particular, viewing the entire closed loop as a single black-box input-output system is extremely powerful for avoiding the identification of high-dimensional physical models.

At the same time, the authors point out several limitations and directions for future work:
- **Handling high-dimensional commands**: The experiments validated relatively low-dimensional command spaces like base velocity (3D) and end-effector position (3D). Adapting to ultra-high-dimensional commands like whole-body joint trajectories will require combining latent-space compression techniques.
- **Computational cost of the optimization backend**: Currently, sampling-based MPPI optimization is used, which can be sensitive to hyperparameter tuning. Since the learned neural network model is differentiable, introducing gradient-based optimization algorithms in the future could solve this faster and more efficiently.
- **Integration with other control frameworks**: While this work focused on reinforcement learning policies, the principle of OSRAM should be directly applicable to classical or model-based controllers like Model Predictive Control (MPC), opening up further applications.

captions.F5: Visualization of OSRAM's error correction mechanism. (a)(b) High 1-step prediction accuracy of the learned closed-loop model. (c)(d) In anticipation of robot tracking lag relative to the dashed target, the purple curve (optimized command) swings wider in advance, resulting in the orange curve (real response) tracking the target closely.

takeaways: Cleverly distorting reference commands before sending them offers an extremely practical third adaptation approach beyond retraining policies or identifying physical parameters on hardware.
Treating inputs and outputs as a single "closed-loop system" of robot and policy yields higher data efficiency and faster online adaptation than modeling full-body physical states.
Pre-training via meta-learning in simulation (e.g., Reptile) allows hardware finetuning to reach sufficient accuracy in just a few dozen gradient updates (a few tens of seconds of data).
Combining OSRAM with existing internal adaptation methods such as RMA holds promise for further tracking performance gains.
limitations: It assumes a low-dimensional command space like base velocity or end-effector position; direct application to high-dimensional tasks that directly command whole-body degrees of freedom is not yet validated.
Because it relies on sampling-based optimization (MPPI), performance is sensitive to the tuning of parameters such as temperature and noise covariance.
It assumes the underlying policy can already execute the task with reasonable stability (without falling); it cannot handle extreme environmental gaps where the policy itself fails catastrophically.
